comments.author: @ComfortablyConstrained
comments.text:
An interesting assessment.  I think that you missed a key point for the US, but your analysis pointed me to it:

A homebuyer in the US gets a 30-year fixed mortgage.  You buy the absolute maximum that you can afford, because your mortgage payment will never go up, and even if your salary only goes up with inflation, the payment still becomes a smaller and smaller percentage of your costs/expenses.

If mortgage rates drop, you refinance and enjoy the lower payment.  If rates increase, you don't ever think about refinancing.

The parents (with mortgages from the low interest rate era) are happy.  Their children, who should be enjoying all of the improvements that you note, are being dragged down by the higher mortgage rates - can't buy, buy with higher costs, and/or buy smaller homes to keep their payments affordable.

It will be interesting to see if younger Americans change their opinions if/when rates come down.  Those with high-rate/payment mortgages will see a reduction in mortgage payments (after they refinance their mortgages) or they might choose to buy a bigger/better house and maintain their payment.  Those who are renting because they cannot afford to buy may be able to buy.  And then they'll all be able to enjoy the other improvements that you noted.

replies.author: @TheLolzKnight
replies.text:
Depends where you live. 

First thing we need to recognize: money is just the way we account for how value is made. A miner digging up ore makes value because people need metal. A barista making coffee makes value because people need coffee. A factory manager who organizes workers better so the same number of workers produce more makes value because people need factory goods. Scientists make new ways to make things, which has value. Artists, truck drivers, any of these. If you do something for a living that makes value: you are labor, congratulations. The total amount of value produced in a country split over the population is what determines the welfare of the population. 

Investors give people money so they can afford the fixed costs (miners pickaxe, the baristas coffee machine, a managers factory building) to be able to do jobs. This is even sometimes labor: ethical investors make their money by figuring out what people need, helping it get made, and then earning back their investment + profit. This doesn't always work and has real risk to it, because you're basically gambling on being able to figure out what people want and need and betting your startup capital on that. And we need someone who can provide investment liquidity to start businesses, so investors.

The problem now is that a lot of investors don't make their money by being smart and figuring out what people need. They make their money by figuring out what people can't go without (housing), or by figuring out an unsustainable way to make value (fossil fuels) and monopolizing+promoting it so extract value from other people for nothing. They didn't make value, they rigged the market using the money they already had. And you can't even get rid of them by refusing to buy from them and going to their competition to start a bidding war. Because they made themselves the only game in town.

Their threat is always "If you take away our rigged system, we'll take our money and leave". Keep in mind that the thing that makes value is people doing work. So frankly? Call their bluff. Ok. Leave. They can't take the houses they want to sell with them. They can't move the factories onto a ship and leave with them. They can't take the people with them either. If they try and destroy the businesses on the way out, make that illegal. This is the equivalent of softly nationalizing these industries, and mandating all businesses in your country are legally required to be worker co-ops would have a similar effect. If they just leave all their money in banks and refuse to spend it? Print more money. Sitting on money and refusing to spend is the same as decreasing the supply of money. If they sell everything they own, buy physical goods to put on a ship and sail somewhere else with? Cool. Tax them on the way out and hey them actually spending the money they have in investments means its circulating the economy and creating demand for valuable things that people can produce! Economy grows as they leave even!

It tends to be a bad idea to be universal and unspecific with stuff like this. My earlier example of a productive investor is a real and very valuable person. Them, or other people who are hard to train need high pay because their jobs are actually hard (doctors) so they don't leave and you don't get brain drain. So it tends to ask that you do massive education spending like training more doctors, lawyers, managers, etc.

The downside of all of that is it ruins foreign investment potential and makes the supply of money worse so you don't have investors anymore who are willing to risk it to invest in future businesses. To which my answer is find or make a new institution to do it. This doesn't mean necessarily a government ran investment bank or something. An institution can mean any system. But all the workers who used to work at the factory still live in your country. Give them a new one! Make is super easy for people with a minimum education level and who are willing to pay a nice but affordable chunk of money to (re)start businesses without the investors. Or do national micro-loans. Look at sectors where the barrier to entry is high and have the national bank say "We will give anyone a grant (0 interest loan) to start a workers co-op that makes this product. You only start paying back the loan after 5 years in business". A clothing factory like that isn't impossible. Make it crazy easy when you see an abusive business model to say "Screw that, I could do that better" and start a competitor. Sure a lot will fail. But just the threat of competition would literally make a lot of these investors behave themselves.

The rule in the economy has to be: If you don't produce value, you can't have shit. Stock markets used to produce value. They got money into the pockets of people who wanted to start a business, or expand their business, who would then go on to produce value. Can we say that about these modern "Investors"? They don't make anything. They shouldn't get paid.

comments.text: You should have tested for the effects of people parking their spare capital in housing stock, often leaving properties empty and thereby restricting the supply of housing. Central banks aim for 2% inflation which means capital loses 2% of its value annually. By investing in real estate, increases in the value of housing stock caused by an annual inflation rate of at least 2% is amplified by the effects of investors parking their unused capital in real estate. The real increase in housing prices is often much higher than the base rate of inflation. This is due to shortages in the supply of housing and the fact that housing is seen as a safe place to park unused capital. This problem is the compounded year upon year. In my view, monetarist policies are in need of urgent review.

comments.text:
Regarding corporate profit ("greed"), it isn't as high as people usually assume

In the world of finance, corporate profit is often measured by the profit margin, meaning:
net profit / sales
That's basically the take a company keeps on what it sells

Across large periods of time it stays remarkably constant, about 6% more or less depending the industry

For supermarkets in the recent years, profit margin hasn't rely climbed that much, and is still below 6% for many large supermarket chains: 2.4% for Tesco UK, 3.1% for Walmart, 0.5% for Carrefour France

What that means for the consumer is that those retailers only keep a few bucks for each 100 spent

Other things though drive price up a lot more: product diversity, perishables, number of customers per shop, etc.
